title: Initialization and Garbage Values
concept: Variables must be initialized before use to avoid unpredictable behavior

steps.title: Including stdio.h Header
steps.explanation:
We import the standard I/O library (```stdio.h```) to use ```printf```. As we learned in the previous lesson, without this line the compiler won't recognize ```printf``` and will throw an error.

This is because the C compiler needs to know the signature (parameters and return type) of a function **before** it is used.

steps.title: Starting the main Function
steps.explanation:
The program entry point. A **main stack frame** (dedicated workspace) is created on the stack. As we learned previously, local variables are stored inside this space.

Right now it's like being assigned an empty locker — soon the two variables ```score``` and ```level``` will go in here.

steps.title: Declaration with Initialization
steps.explanation:
`int score = 100;` is the safest pattern — it declares and initializes in one step.

If you delay initialization, there's a danger zone until the value is actually assigned. That's why the best habit is to use the form `type variable = initialValue;`.

steps.title: Declaration Only (Garbage Value)
steps.explanation:
`int level;` only allocates space without storing a value.

Reading `level` in this state can lead to undefined behavior, so it's safer to initialize immediately like `int level = 1;`.

steps.title: Assignment
steps.explanation:
`level = 1;` overwrites the previous garbage state with an actual value.

`=` is the assignment operator, not a comparison — it stores the result of the right side into the variable on the left.

steps.title: Printing Variable Values
steps.explanation:
In `printf("Score: %d, Level: %d\n", score, level);`, the two `%d` placeholders are filled with values in order.

If the number of format specifiers doesn't match the number of arguments, you'll get incorrect output or bugs.

steps.title: Program Termination
steps.explanation:
`return 0;` terminates the program normally and cleans up main's local variables.

In summary, initializing variables at the time of declaration is the most basic safety measure in C.

quiz.question: What problem occurs when you forget to initialize a variable?
options: Garbage values cause unexpected results or bugs
quiz.explanation:
Most modern compilers will give a warning, but the code still compiles and runs.
This can cause unpredictable behavior (Undefined Behavior).

misconceptions.wrong: I'll assign a value later, so just declaring is fine
misconceptions.correct: Whenever possible, initialize with a default like `int a = 0;`.
misconceptions.why: As code gets longer, it's easy to forget where (or whether) you initialized a variable.

keyTakeaway: Initialize at declaration. That's the safest approach.
